strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: improving program runtime beyond compiler optimization. Constructing training pairs across programmers is a simple, potentially useful data-curation strategy.

The reported improvements are substantial. For DeepSeek-Coder 33B at BEST@8, PIE-Problem increases the optimization rate from 51.76% to 71.03% and average speedup from 2.649× to 4.812×; linear merging further improves these to 76.65% and 5.087×.

Evaluation includes two model families, multiple model sizes, and both single-sample and eight-sample generation. Problem-disjoint splits, correctness testing, compilation with -O3, and deterministic simulation are useful experimental choices. Reporting correctness separately makes the optimization–correctness tradeoff visible.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate the proposed problem-oriented perspective. PIE-Problem simultaneously changes programmer pairing, the runtime-reduction threshold from over 10% to over 90%, training size, problem coverage, and prompting. Matched-threshold, matched-problem, matched-size, and matched-prompt controls are needed to establish whether cross-programmer pairing itself drives the gains rather than selecting much faster training targets.

Evidence for global algorithmic innovation is weaker than claimed. The optimization-category analysis lacks annotator details and agreement measurements, and it examines training pairs rather than generated optimizations. Some illustrative analyses are inaccurate: Figure 2 shows linear-time approaches throughout, while Figure 10(b) already appears linear because its inner counter advances monotonically across the outer loop, contrary to the stated O(N log N) complexity. These examples weaken the proposed distinction between local iteration and algorithmic innovation.

The model-merging contribution applies established methods without sufficient comparison to simpler alternatives. Joint training on a mixture of PIE-User and PIE-Problem, merging toward the original checkpoint, and allocating a fixed sampling budget across the two constituent models would help establish the specific value of merging complementary optimization behaviors. Sequential training alone does not resolve this question.

Correctness remains a substantial limitation. The final DeepSeek-Coder 33B model achieves only 48.03% correctness at BEST@1 and 78.76% at BEST@8, below the corresponding PIE-User results of 59.49% and 91.14%. BEST@8 selects candidates using all evaluation tests and measured runtime, while incorrect or slower outputs receive a fallback speedup of 1.0. This is a useful oracle-assisted optimization metric, but does not establish reliable deployment performance; separate selection and held-out correctness tests are needed.

Evaluation is confined to one C++ competitive-programming benchmark containing 80 test problems. There are no repeated-run uncertainties, problem-level confidence intervals, speedup distributions, or native-hardware validation. Arithmetic mean speedup can be dominated by a few large gains, and 1,422 program pairs should not be treated as independent problem-level evidence.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the claimed public release: the manuscript supplies no identifiable project artifact link. It also omits important details such as exact checkpoint identifiers, batch size and sequence length, simulator configuration, selected merge weights and their validation procedure, and the self-correction protocol.

Overall novelty is modest: the contribution combines a straightforward reconstruction of an existing dataset with standard fine-tuning and model merging. The promising numerical results warrant further investigation, but the missing causal controls and limited validation leave the central claims insufficiently supported for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: improving program runtime beyond compiler optimizations. Constructing training pairs across programmers solving the same problem is a simple, potentially valuable data-curation approach.

The reported gains are substantial across two model families and several sizes. For DeepSeek-Coder 33B at BEST@8, PIE-Problem increases optimization success from 51.76% to 71.03% and average speedup from 2.649× to 4.812×; model merging further improves these to 76.65% and 5.087×.

The evaluation preserves the original validation/test sets, explicitly separates problem IDs across splits, checks generated programs against tests, and measures performance with gem5 under compiler optimization. Reporting both BEST@1 and BEST@8, correctness, and unsuccessful-generation categories provides useful context.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not isolate the proposed contribution. PIE-Problem changes cross-user pairing, the runtime-reduction threshold from >10% to >90%, training-set size, problem coverage, and prompting simultaneously. Matched comparisons controlling these factors—especially high-speedup filtering of PIE-User and threshold sweeps for both pairing strategies—are necessary to establish that cross-user pairing drives the improvement.

The evidence for global algorithmic innovation contains technical errors. Figure 2 shows linear-time methods throughout and primarily illustrates eliminating a prefix-sum pass/storage. More decisively, Figure 10(b) already runs in O(N): its condition check is constant-time and the shared 'now' variable advances at most N times across all outer iterations. The caption incorrectly labels it O(N log N), overstating the advantage of the cross-user solution. Figure 3 also lacks annotator agreement and a sufficiently detailed labeling protocol; a large runtime reduction alone does not establish algorithmic innovation.

The model-merging contribution applies existing techniques without the baselines needed to explain its benefit. Missing comparisons include joint training on a controlled mixture of both datasets and interpolation with the pretrained base model. These would help distinguish complementary optimization knowledge from ordinary regularization or recovery of capabilities lost during fine-tuning. The explanations involving cognitive inertia and fixed thinking patterns remain speculative.

Practical reliability remains weak. DeepSeek-Coder 33B's BEST@1 correctness falls from 59.49% on PIE-User to 37.41% on PIE-Problem and recovers only to 48.03% after linear merging. BEST@8 selects the fastest candidate using the same tests used for evaluation, and unsuccessful candidates receive fallback speedup 1.0. This is a useful oracle-assisted optimization protocol, but independent correctness tests and selection-cost measurements are needed to substantiate deployment claims.

Evaluation is confined to one C++ competitive-programming benchmark with 80 test problems. There are no repeated-run uncertainty estimates, problem-level aggregation, or speedup-distribution analyses, despite multiple correlated samples per problem and an arithmetic mean that can be dominated by large improvements. Generalization to other workloads and actual hardware is not demonstrated.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript states that data, code, and evaluation scripts are public but supplies no identifiable release link. Important details are missing, including the gem5 configuration, exact model checkpoints, batch size and sequence limits, the merging procedure for LoRA-trained models, and the validation-based rule for selecting merge weights. The self-correction baseline is also insufficiently specified.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: improving program runtime through transformations beyond compiler optimization. Constructing training pairs across different programmers is intuitive and potentially useful.

The reported gains are substantial. For DeepSeek-Coder 33B at BEST@8, PIE-Problem improves optimization rate from 51.76% to 71.03% and average speedup from 2.649× to 4.812×; linear merging further improves these to 76.65% and 5.087×.

Experiments cover two model families and multiple model sizes, with prompting, fine-tuning, self-correction, and sequential training comparisons. Reporting both BEST@1 and BEST@8 helps characterize sampling benefits.

The evaluation preserves the original benchmark splits, explicitly separates problems across splits, checks generated programs against tests, and measures performance with gem5 after GCC -O3 optimization. The correctness analysis also exposes an important tradeoff.
weaknesses: The central comparison is substantially confounded. PIE-Problem changes the pairing policy, runtime-reduction threshold from greater than 10% to greater than 90%, training size from 56,086 to 14,051 pairs, problem coverage from 1,135 to 336 problems, and training prompt. Without matched-threshold, matched-problem, matched-size, and matched-prompt controls, the results cannot establish that cross-programmer pairing drives the gains rather than selecting much faster targets.

The technical contribution is primarily data re-pairing and filtering followed by established model-merging methods. The merging experiments omit important alternatives, including jointly training on both datasets and merging the PIE-Problem model with its original base model. Consequently, they do not establish whether complementary optimization knowledge is responsible for the gains, rather than a more general interpolation or regularization effect.

Correctness remains a substantial limitation. For DeepSeek-Coder 33B, BEST@1 correctness falls from 59.49% with PIE-User to 37.41% with PIE-Problem, and merging restores it only to 48.03%. BEST@8 selects the fastest candidate using all evaluation tests, without a separate held-out test set for assessing the selected program. These results support optimization under test-based selection, but provide weaker evidence of reliable semantic preservation or deployment performance.

Evidence for global algorithmic innovation is insufficient. A greater-than-90% runtime reduction does not itself establish an algorithmic change, and the annotation study lacks annotator counts, agreement statistics, and a detailed adjudication protocol. Figure 2's examples all have linear time complexity and mainly differ in passes and intermediate storage. The paper also does not systematically classify the transformations generated by the trained models, so the dataset analysis does not establish that models learned more global algorithmic improvements.

Evaluation is restricted to one competitive-programming benchmark with 80 test problems. There are no repeated-run uncertainties, problem-level confidence intervals, or speedup distributions; arithmetic mean speedup can be dominated by a few large gains. Independent benchmarks and real-hardware measurements would strengthen the broader practical claims.

Reproducibility details are incomplete despite the claim that resources are publicly available: the manuscript provides no identifiable project link, exact checkpoint identifiers, complete training configuration, gem5 configuration, or detailed self-correction procedure. It also does not clearly explain how merge weights were selected using validation data. These omissions, together with the missing causal controls, leave the promising empirical results insufficiently supported for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: improving program runtime through high-level transformations beyond compiler optimization. Pairing solutions from different programmers is a simple, practical way to obtain richer optimization supervision.

Table 1 reports substantial, consistent gains across five model configurations. For Qwen2.5-Coder 32B, PCO increases BEST@1 optimization rate from 31.24% to 58.89% and average speedup from 2.95× to 5.22×.

The comparison matches training-pair counts per problem, uses problem-disjoint splits, and evaluates with gem5 and GCC -O3. The data-efficiency experiment provides additional evidence that PCO is useful.

Anchor verification improves results across three refinement models and both training datasets. Training settings and prompts are provided, and the paper explicitly reports correctness alongside performance.
weaknesses: The central experiment does not isolate the proposed explanation for PCO's gains. PCO selects the highest-speedup pairs from an expanded candidate pool, changing target quality, source-program distribution, and programmer diversity simultaneously. Matching pair counts alone does not control these factors. Speedup-matched comparisons, fixed-source pairing, and random versus top-speedup cross-user selection are needed to establish the contribution of cross-programmer diversity.

Anchor verification is essentially differential testing against a reference implementation followed by execution-guided repair. Its novelty is overstated and insufficiently positioned against established testing methods. The baselines omit random or coverage-guided input generation using the same reference oracle, and there is no ablation of code explanation or test count. Consequently, the experiments do not establish which proposed components add value beyond using executable ground truth.

Evaluation covers only 41 distinct test problems from one competitive-programming benchmark. The 978 pairs are not independent problem instances, yet no problem-level uncertainty, seed variation, or per-problem results are reported. Arithmetic mean speedup can be dominated by a few large improvements; medians, distributions, and an independent benchmark would materially strengthen the evidence.

The reported performance metrics rely on oracle information: BEST@8 selects the fastest candidate passing all evaluation tests, and incorrect or slower candidates receive a speedup of 1.0×. This is a stated benchmark convention, but it does not demonstrate deployable performance with the proposed three-test verifier. The paper should report incorrect candidates accepted by that verifier, fallback behavior, performance regressions, and refinement costs. Even the strongest refinement result leaves 25.46% of outputs incorrect, so claims that the process ensures correctness are unsupported.

The evidence for global algorithmic innovation is weaker than presented. CFG edit distance and t-SNE dispersion can reflect coding style or program size rather than algorithmic improvements, while the small human study lacks annotator and agreement details. Some illustrative complexity claims are incorrect: Figure 18(b) has a monotonically increasing inner-loop variable and linear total loop work, contrary to its O(N log N) description; Figure 16's fixed-state dynamic programs are already O(N). These errors weaken the proposed distinction between local and global optimization.

Important construction and reproducibility details remain ambiguous. The text describes adjacent submission pairs, but its counting formulas use all combinations with an unexplained factor of one-half. Input-validity filtering, runtime-ranking reliability, deduplication, and evaluation-test coverage are insufficiently specified. These details matter because accepted submissions and successful execution on generated inputs do not establish semantic equivalence over valid inputs.

The paper does not adequately position this contribution against that established approach or compare against random, mutation-based, or coverage-guided input generation using the same reference program.

Correctness claims exceed the evidence. The framework generates only three inputs and performs at most one refinement iteration; its best reported correctness is 74.54%. Executing the original program supplies an oracle only for valid inputs and defined behavior, while input-domain validation is insufficiently specified. Evaluation breadth and uncertainty are inadequate for the general claims. The 978 test examples cover only 41 competitive-programming problems in C++, with no independent benchmark, repeated-run uncertainty, or problem-level confidence intervals. The arithmetic mean speedup can be dominated by a few large gains; per-problem results, speedup distributions, and native-hardware measurements would strengthen the evidence.

The reported metrics leave a gap between benchmark gains and practical deployment. BEST@8 selects the fastest candidate passing all evaluation tests, providing oracle selection. Assigning incorrect or slower outputs a speedup of 1× also presumes successful fallback detection. The paper should evaluate selection and fallback using only available verification tests, report missed errors, and quantify generation and verification costs.

Larger CFG edit distances and dispersed t-SNE embeddings can reflect stylistic changes rather than improved algorithms, and the human study lacks annotation-agreement details. Figure 18 incorrectly describes version (b) as O(N log N): its constant-time check and monotonically increasing inner-loop variable give O(N) total work, so the same user's revision already makes the claimed asymptotic improvement.

Construction and implementation details contain unresolved ambiguities. Section 3.1 describes sequential pairing but gives combinatorial counts with an unexplained factor of one-half. Runtime provenance, tie handling, deduplication, input filtering, and gem5 configuration are not sufficiently specified to reproduce the full pipeline.

The related work and baselines do not adequately position this contribution against reference-based testing, fuzzing, or other code-optimization methods beyond PIE.

Evaluation diversity remains limited: the C++ test set contains 978 examples but only 41 distinct problems, and Python remains within CodeNet. Practical performance claims overstate the evaluation protocol. BEST@k selects the fastest candidate passing the evaluation tests, while the speedup metric assigns incorrect or slower outputs 1×. These are useful benchmark conventions, but they assume knowledge of failures that the deployed verifier may miss. Performance under selection and fallback using only generated anchor tests, followed by independent held-out evaluation, is needed.

The correctness guarantees of anchor tests are overstated. Executing the original program establishes reference agreement for particular inputs, not input validity or semantic equivalence. Only three inputs are generated, input filtering is underspecified, and coverage and false-acceptance rates are not measured. Comparison with budget-matched random or coverage-guided reference testing would clarify the LLM test generator's value.

Evidence for learning transferable algorithmic transformations is weaker than claimed. GED and t-SNE dispersion can reflect style or implementation differences, and Appendix O provides only one illustrative case. Some supporting explanations are technically inaccurate: Figure 19(b) already uses constant-time checks with a monotonically advancing counter, yielding linear total complexity rather than the stated O(N log N); Figure 22's erroneous termination condition causes nontermination at mx = n−1, rather than premature stopping.

Reproducibility and dataset construction need greater precision. Sequential-pair descriptions conflict with combinatorial pair-count formulas, whose extra factor of one-half is unexplained. Runtime ranking, tie handling, deduplication, test-suite construction, and gem5 configuration are insufficiently documented, and no code or dataset release location is provided.

The evaluation includes meaningful controls: matched training-pair counts per problem, problem-disjoint splits, random versus top-speedup sampling, GED-stratified subsets, and reduced-data experiments. Appendix H provides evidence that gains are not solely due to top-speedup selection.

Anchor verification improves results across three refinement models, with additional experiments on iteration count, output-generation accuracy, Python, and execution overhead. Training settings and prompts provide useful reproducibility details.
weaknesses: Novelty is insufficiently established. Cross-user pairing is a straightforward extension of existing optimization datasets, while executing a reference implementation to obtain expected outputs is an established differential-testing technique. The paper does not adequately position anchor verification against this literature or compare against reference-based random, mutation-based, or coverage-guided testing.

Evaluation breadth is limited despite the many experimental variants: the C++ test set contains 978 pairs from only 41 problems. There are no problem-level confidence intervals, repeated-run uncertainty estimates, or independent benchmark evaluations. Python remains within CodeNet, and hardware validation covers only 20 selected pairs.

The practical interpretation of the metrics is too strong. BEST@k selects the fastest candidate passing the evaluation tests, while SPEEDUP assigns 1× to incorrect or slower outputs, implicitly assuming reliable fallback. These are useful benchmark conventions but do not establish deployable selection performance. Selection using generated tests followed by independent held-out evaluation, including false-acceptance rates, is needed.

Anchor verification uses only three generated inputs, with no test-budget or coverage study. Executing the original program establishes reference outputs for those inputs, not semantic equivalence; filtering malformed inputs also does not establish that inputs satisfy the problem's semantic constraints. C++ correctness remains 74.54% after one refinement and 79.24% after five, limiting the claimed practicality.

The explanation that PCO teaches transferable algorithmic edit patterns exceeds the evidence. CFG edit distance and t-SNE dispersion do not distinguish algorithmic improvement from implementation variation, and Appendix O provides only an illustrative case. Figure 16 also labels a change between linear-time implementations as a more efficient algorithm without isolating algorithmic versus implementation effects.

Several methodological details remain ambiguous: sequential-pair construction is inconsistent with the combinatorial pair-count discussion; test-suite size and adequacy, input-validity filtering, runtime-label reliability, and key gem5 settings are insufficiently specified. These gaps weaken reproducibility and confidence in the correctness and performance claims.

strengths: The problem-oriented training construction is simple, useful, and supported by substantial improvements across five model configurations. For Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, optimization success increases from 31.24% to 58.90%, with reported mean speedup increasing from 2.95× to 5.22×.

The matched-data ablation meaningfully supports the central contribution: randomly sampled problem-oriented pairs achieve 49.55% optimization success versus 26.96% for PIE, showing that selecting the highest-speedup pairs is not the sole explanation.

Anchor verification consistently improves correctness and optimization performance across three refinement models. The controlled comparison using identical inputs with model-generated versus executed outputs helps establish the benefit of reliable test outputs.

The evaluation includes problem-disjoint splits, Python experiments, data-efficiency studies, refinement-iteration ablations, and limited physical-hardware validation. Together, these provide concrete evidence supporting a marginal acceptance.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate. Cross-user pairing expands an existing supervised optimization setup, while anchor verification applies the established principle of differential testing against a reference implementation. The related-work discussion and baselines do not adequately establish its advance over reference-based testing, fuzzing, or repair using existing regression tests.

The C++ test set contains 978 pairs but only 41 independent problems. No problem-level confidence intervals, repeated-training variability, or per-problem results are reported. Pair-averaged results can overweight particular problems, and arithmetic mean speedup can be dominated by a few large improvements.

BEST@k selects the fastest candidate passing the evaluation tests, and the speedup metric assigns 1.0× to incorrect or slower outputs. These are useful oracle-assisted benchmark metrics, but they do not establish achievable deployment performance. Evaluation should separately measure selection using generated tests, correctness on held-out tests, and undetected regressions.

Anchor verification generates only three inputs per example, and input validation is described primarily in terms of format. Executing the original program does not establish that an input satisfies the problem's semantic constraints. Coverage, invalid-input rates, and false acceptance rates are not measured; 74.54% correctness after one refinement still leaves substantial practical risk.

Several interpretations exceed the evidence. CFG distance and embedding dispersion do not establish algorithmic innovation, and the single prefix-sum case study does not demonstrate robust learning of transferable edit patterns. Hardware validation covers only 20 pairs, while generalization to repository-scale software remains speculative. Reproduction would also benefit from released construction scripts, exact evaluation-test details, and fuller execution and training configurations.
